title: NVDA Stock Tests $200 Support as Political Backlash Hits Nvidia and Chip Sector - FXLeaders
content: Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) shares have reversed towards $200 as Democratic victories in the US midterm elections raise concerns about political opposition to data-centre expansion, while rising financing costs, infrastructure constraints and growing competition add pressure to the semiconductor sector. Nvidia shares have struggled to maintain their recovery after retreating from record highs above $243. The stock initially rebounded from the $200 level on Tuesday, climbing towards $210 as improving geopolitical sentiment provided some support for technology shares. However, the recovery quickly lost momentum as investors reassessed the sustainability of enormous infrastructure spending commitments. The latest Democratic election victories have added another challenge, sending chipmakers and companies connected to data-centre construction lower. Nvidia is particularly exposed to these developments because its growth expectations depend heavily on continued investment by major cloud providers and technology companies. The stock is now testing support around $200. A decisive break below this level could expose further downside towards $180, while buyers need to reclaim $210 to improve the immediate technical outlook. The political landscape has become increasingly important for Nvidia and the wider semiconductor industry. Democratic victories in several key states have strengthened opposition to rapid data-centre expansion, particularly in Texas. Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Greg Abbott, becoming Texas’s first Democratic governor in more than three decades. During her campaign, Hinojosa advocated an immediate freeze on new data-centre developments. Similar concerns are emerging in Ohio and Georgia, where Governor-elect Amy Acton and Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms have also campaigned against unchecked digital infrastructure growth. These developments do not necessarily mean existing projects will be cancelled, but tighter permitting requirements, electricity restrictions and construction delays could complicate future expansion. For Nvidia, the concern is that political resistance could eventually affect the pace of infrastructure investment and demand for its advanced processors. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s reported involvement in Marvell Technology’s acquisition of Lumentum Holdings highlights the company’s growing influence across the semiconductor supply chain. According to Bloomberg, Marvell CEO Matthew Murphy and Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston consulted Huang before announcing the transaction, which values Lumentum at approximately $115 billion in enterprise value. Nvidia previously invested $2 billion in each company, strengthening its relationships with suppliers involved in optical networking and data-centre connectivity. While the deal reinforces Nvidia’s strategic influence, its enormous size also highlights the capital requirements and financing risks associated with expanding the infrastructure supporting advanced computing. NVIDIA shares lost momentum early in September after failing to break decisively above the $236 resistance zone, with the rejection sending the stock back below $210 but we have seen a decent rebound recently. Shares have climbed above $233 today as investors responded positively to expanding infrastructure partnerships and CEO projections, but buyers are not able to sustain the rally above $243 and we saw dive to $200 again last week but we saw some improvement yesterday as NVDA finds support at the 50 weekly SMA. However we’re back at the 50 SMA today. Despite growing concerns, demand for computing capacity remains substantial. Reports indicate that Anthropic plans to increase its computing capacity beyond 3.5 gigawatts by the end of 2026, potentially reaching approximately 7 gigawatts in 2027. Such expansion highlights the enormous infrastructure requirements associated with developing and operating increasingly sophisticated models, providing continued support for Nvidia’s longer-term growth prospects. Samsung Electronics is also reportedly preparing to manufacture base dies for high-bandwidth memory chips intended for Nvidia and AMD at its second foundry facility in Taylor, Texas. Construction is expected to begin this month, with mass production targeted for 2030. Competition is another growing concern. Google and Oracle have announced plans to make Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) available through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure from 2027. This gives customers another option beyond Nvidia-powered systems, as major technology companies increasingly look to develop custom processors to reduce computing costs and dependence on external suppliers. Nvidia retains considerable advantages through its established software ecosystem, performance and customer relationships. However, expanding competition could eventually put pressure on pricing and market share, even if overall computing demand continues growing. ASML reported record third-quarter sales of €11.7 billion but warned that semiconductor manufacturing capacity planned for 2027 and 2028 might not fully satisfy anticipated demand. The company forecast fourth-quarter revenue of €14.2 billion to €15.2 billion and narrowed its 2026 sales guidance to €44 billion–€45 billion. Although manufacturing constraints could support semiconductor pricing, they could also delay production expansion and complicate Nvidia’s supply arrangements. Financing is another concern. CoreWeave has experienced pressure as yields on its $1.25 billion bond issue due in 2032 reportedly climbed towards 15%. Such borrowing costs highlight the risks facing companies investing heavily in data-centre infrastructure. Electricity shortages are also creating deployment problems. Amazon reportedly has Nvidia-equipped server racks waiting in warehouses because some facilities lack sufficient electricity to operate them. Delays could increase storage costs and postpone revenue generation from infrastructure investments. Nvidia continues to benefit from substantial long-term computing demand, expanding customer relationships and its dominant position in advanced processors. However, the market is increasingly questioning whether infrastructure investment can maintain its previous growth trajectory. The Democratic midterm victories introduce another layer of uncertainty, with potential restrictions on data-centre construction adding to concerns about financing, electricity availability and competition. Technically, $200 is the immediate support level to watch. A sustained break below it could expose $180, while a recovery above $210 would provide an initial indication that buyers are regaining control. For now, the balance of risks has shifted towards sellers. Nvidia’s longer-term growth prospects remain significant, but investors may become less willing to pay premium valuations if political resistance and infrastructure costs begin threatening the expansion plans underpinning semiconductor earnings.

For readers following US Technical Analysis, the move raises a central question: is this the start of a renewed uptrend, or a relief rally within a broader correction? The Nasdaq tech index, which includes Nvidia as one of its largest components, remains in correction territory after falling meaningfully from its recent high. That backdrop shapes how traders interpret every bounce in leading technology stocks. Chip stocks fell sharply in late October after Intel's weak forecast triggered a sector-wide slump. Concerns about costly AI investments, stretched valuations and mixed outlooks from some large technology companies added to the pressure. Nvidia was caught in that wave despite strong demand for its AI accelerators. When markets de-risk, the largest and most widely owned names often fall alongside the sector, regardless of company-specific fundamentals. Results from major cloud providers this season showed rapid growth in AI-related spending and rising capital expenditure plans. Much of that spending flows to AI chips and networking, which supports demand for Nvidia's products. Nvidia's longer-term trend remains upward, with the stock still trading well above its levels from a year ago. The recent pullback created a series of lower highs over several weeks, a pattern technical analysts associate with a short-term correction within a larger uptrend. The rebound has brought the stock back toward its short-term moving averages, which may act as resistance. A decisive move above these levels, ideally on rising volume, would suggest demand for the shares is returning. On the downside, traders are watching the recent swing low formed during the late-October slump. If that level stays intact on any retest, it would form a new base, often described as a higher low, which can mark the end of a correction. The longer-term moving average remains an important reference. As long as the stock stays above it, many technical traders view the primary trend as intact. A sustained break below it would signal a more serious shift. Momentum indicators have recovered from oversold levels reached during the slump, suggesting downside pressure has eased. However, momentum has not yet returned to strong bullish territory, consistent with a market still searching for direction. Volume patterns will be important. Rallies on heavy volume tend to be more durable than those on light trading, so traders will watch participation closely in the coming sessions. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results later in November, an event that often drives large price moves. Options markets typically imply significant volatility around the release. Strong guidance may help the stock break out of its recent range, while any disappointment may push it back toward support. Because Nvidia carries a large weight in major indices, its post-earnings move can influence the direction of the broader market. The US midterm elections, interest rate expectations and energy prices are also influencing sentiment. Election-related volatility and shifting expectations for Federal Reserve policy may add noise to price action in the near term. Technical traders often wait for these macro events to pass before committing to new positions, which may keep the stock range-bound until the earnings release. The strength of the broader semiconductor group matters for Nvidia's chart. On the rebound day, many chip stocks advanced together, suggesting broad participation rather than gains concentrated in a few names. Broad participation tends to support more durable rallies. If the sector continues to recover, Nvidia may benefit from renewed flows into AI-related stocks. If breadth narrows again, the rebound may struggle to extend. Long-term investors often focus less on short-term chart patterns and more on demand for AI infrastructure, which remains strong according to recent results from major cloud providers. Even so, technical levels influence trading behaviour around key events such as earnings. Seasonal patterns can also play a role. The final months of the year have often been supportive for technology stocks, though past patterns offer no guarantee of future performance. As one of the largest companies in the Nasdaq Composite, Nvidia's chart is closely tied to the direction of the AI trade. The rebound is encouraging, but resistance overhead and a correcting Nasdaq tech index suggest caution. The upcoming earnings report is likely to determine whether the stock resumes its uptrend or extends its consolidation. title: Where Could NVIDIA’s Next Growth Come From? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. NVIDIA (NVDA) reported revenue of $96.2 billion in fiscal Q2 2027, up 105.9% from a year earlier. Management expects revenue to grow about 70% in fiscal 2028, and said supply constraints limit that forecast. During the August 26, 2026 call detailing these projections, management said NVIDIA had just begun shipping a new generation of data center hardware. What is that hardware, and are customers buying it yet? The new hardware is Vera Rubin, and customers placed orders before the first units left. Management said production shipments began in August 2026. By then, NVIDIA already had purchase orders from every major AI cloud and system maker, along with every major hyperscaler, as the largest cloud companies are known. Management expects Vera Rubin to be the fastest product ramp in NVIDIA’s history, which is a forecast, not a result. Vera Rubin operates as a whole system rather than a single chip. The architecture spans the Vera CPU, the Rubin GPU, networking equipment and the Groq LPU. For every gigawatt of AI data center capacity built with Vera Rubin, management puts NVIDIA’s revenue opportunity at $40 billion. That compares with $25 billion for Blackwell, the generation before it. Management also named one large buyer. AWS is deploying an additional 2 million NVIDIA GPUs from fiscal Q3 2027 through fiscal Q2 2029, alongside Vera CPUs, some of them integrated with Rubin. How Much Of NVIDIA’s Business Could Vera Rubin Become? Management said Vera Rubin is expected to make up about 20% of NVIDIA’s data center revenue in fiscal Q3 2027, its first quarter of shipments. That represents a fifth of the business driving most of NVIDIA’s sales. Data center revenue reached $89 billion in fiscal Q2 2027, up 18% from the previous quarter. For fiscal Q3 2027 as a whole, management expects total sales of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%. NVIDIA’s next earnings report is due on November 17, 2026. Vera Rubin is not a side product at a large company. It serves as the next version of the hardware NVIDIA already sells most of, and NVIDIA’s Compute & Networking segment made up 89.6% of company revenue in fiscal 2026. The share price has not kept pace with the sales. NVIDIA stock ended November 3, 2026, trading 13.6% below its highest close of the past year, set on October 6. Over the year to November 3, the stock returned 2.3%, compared with 11.9% for the S&P 500. At 25.9 times trailing earnings, against 22.8 for the S&P 500, the stock trades at only a small premium to the market, which suggests investors expect NVIDIA’s growth to slow well below the 83.4% revenue growth of the past twelve months. Supply could. Management expects supply to remain a bottleneck at least through the end of fiscal 2028, meaning NVIDIA’s sales are limited by what it can get made, not by orders alone. Costs are rising too. Memory prices have climbed more than management expected, and management now sees gross margin bottoming at 71% to 72% in fiscal Q4 2027. Management expects margins to settle at 72% to 73% in fiscal 2028, once price increases it has already put through take effect. Then there is the question of who pays for the hardware. NVIDIA has invested nearly $50 billion in frontier AI labs, and plans to back some of their purchases with its own balance sheet. Management expects demand from those labs to make up roughly a quarter of its business in fiscal 2028, and said on the call that some will call this circular financing. Vera Rubin’s share of data center revenue, measured against management’s guide, is the number to watch in NVIDIA’s next earnings report. Nvidia invented the GPU, the chip behind nearly every major AI system on the planet. But it’s so much more today. It sells entire “AI factories” in a box: multi-rack systems packed with processors, memory, servers, cooling, and the high-speed networking that lets everything work together like one big “brain.” And its CUDA software is so deeply embedded across every cloud, AI lab, and frontier model that it’s become the de facto AI infrastructure operating system. Nvidia grew revenue 106% year over year from $46.7 billion to $96.2 billion in fiscal Q2 2027 (ended July 26, 2026). That’s unprecedented. No public company in history has ever organically doubled quarterly revenue from such a large base. Nvidia’s “Data Center” revenue, which is the AI business, grew 117% year over year in Q2 to $89 billion. The company guided for total revenue of $108 billion this quarter, which would be its first $100 billion quarter. It also guided for 70% revenue growth in fiscal 2028, which is basically calendar year 2027. And the cap on that growth guidance is supply, not demand. The company said it would have been about double again absent the supply crunch. Meanwhile, the customer list has broadened considerably. For two years, the most popular argument against Nvidia was basically: “Its whole business depends on four giant customers, all of which are building their own chips to become less reliant on Nvidia.” It’s true that these four “hyperscalers”—Amazon, Microsoft, Google (GOOGL), and Meta Platforms (META)—have been driving much of the AI infrastructure buildout. They’ll continue to do so for at least a few more years. And all four are indeed building their own AI chips these days. But as the hyperscalers have increased their AI spending, so have lots of other companies. Governments around the world have too for their “sovereign AI” initiatives. And we now have a lot more color on that broadening AI spending… In Q1, Nvidia started separating its AI revenue into two buckets. Bucket one is the hyperscalers. Bucket two is everybody else, which Nvidia calls ACIE (short for AI Clouds, Industrial, and Enterprise). So ACIE covers the neoclouds, governments, hospitals, banks, carmakers, drug companies, AI startups, etc. Meanwhile, most of the customers in the faster-growing ACIE bucket will never even think about designing their own chips. What’s more, the hyperscalers have shown no signs of pulling back yet. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress said it clearly on the call: “With cloud industry backlog now greater than $2 trillion, CapEx by the top five hyperscalers is expected to reach nearly $800 billion in 2026 and $1.3 trillion in 2027.” (Oracle is the fifth hyperscaler she referred to.) And Amazon—which does design its own AI chips and has basically been Exhibit A for the whole “hyperscalers will defect” thesis—committed to deploying another 2 million Nvidia GPUs through 2028. Amazon is also adopting Nvidia’s full physical AI stack (Omniverse, Cosmos, Isaac, and Jetson) to power its fleet of warehouse robots. So the giants are still buying from Nvidia, a new class of customer has shown up behind them, and both are compounding at once. First, the Vera Rubin ramp. Nvidia expects supply to stay tight through at least fiscal 2028 (basically calendar 2027). We want to see the company deliver at least the 70% growth it expects. I also want gross margin to bottom in the 71% to 72% range. If it falls below that threshold, it means memory costs are temporarily winning the tug-of-war Second, how much Nvidia invests in, guarantees, and backstops its customers. It has about $165 billion in these types of financing arrangements. Critics call this “circular financing.” But we’re not concerned. Those guarantees are only about 1.3X Nvidia’s trailing 12-month free cash flow… and only about half of our two-year forward annual free cash flow forecast. What’s more, if a customer fails, what’s left behind is Nvidia equipment that other buyers are lining up for, not dark fiber like after the dot-com bust. Third, the Open Agent Safety Platform Nvidia launched just this week. It’s a two-piece (hardware and software) system for keeping AI agents inside the boundaries set by operators. The launch follows disclosures from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google of recent incidents in which their AI models escaped their test sandboxes—during testing with safeguards reduced, I should add—and hacked other organizations. Nvidia says that from what it knows about the most notorious of such incidents—OpenAI’s models breaching Hugging Face—this new platform could have stopped it. The significance: Nvidia is basically trying to make its hardware the place where AI agent safety lives. And it’s giving away the software layer to make that architecture the industry default—the classic CUDA-style playbook applied to safety. It strengthens the “you need the whole Nvidia stack” narrative and gives CEO Jensen Huang a powerful talking point and a place at the table on one of the industry’s biggest problems. But it’s effectively an “option” on the future, not a moat today. And the open design means the door is deliberately left open for others. P.S. title: NVDA Stock Rebounds Off $200 Support after the Nvidia CEO Comments and Anthropic Expansion - FXLeaders
content: Nvidia stock recovered approximately 3% after retreating toward $200, as improving geopolitical sentiment supports technology stocks, while Big Tech earnings, rising infrastructure costs, custom-chip competition and financing risks continue to challenge the semiconductor sector Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) shares have struggled to maintain their upward momentum after retreating from record highs above $243, falling toward $200 as disappointing Big Tech earnings and concerns about infrastructure spending weighed on semiconductor stocks. The stock recently recovered toward $220 after finding support around $210, but the rebound lost momentum as investors reassessed the sustainability of technology companies’ enormous infrastructure commitments. Nvidia is now attempting another recovery, gaining approximately 3% as improving sentiment surrounding the Middle East conflict supports broader market sentiment. Comments from President Trump during a Fox News interview concerning Israel and the conflict with Iran have encouraged expectations that Washington could pursue a diplomatic agreement with Tehran. The prospect of de-escalation has also contributed to downward pressure on oil prices, helping improve sentiment across financial markets. However, the broader semiconductor outlook remains complicated. Strong demand for processors and memory does not necessarily guarantee continued earnings growth, particularly when customers must secure financing, electricity and operational capacity to deploy increasingly expensive computing infrastructure. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s reported involvement in Marvell Technology’s acquisition of Lumentum Holdings has highlighted Nvidia’s growing influence across the semiconductor supply chain. According to Bloomberg, Marvell CEO Matthew Murphy and Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston consulted Huang before announcing the transaction, which values Lumentum at an enterprise value of approximately $115 billion. Nvidia previously invested $2 billion in each company, strengthening its financial relationships with suppliers involved in optical networking and data-centre connectivity. The development highlights how Nvidia is expanding its influence beyond processors, although the enormous transaction also raises questions about financing, integration and the capital required to expand infrastructure. Nvidia has received additional support from reports that Anthropic plans to significantly expand its computing capacity. According to a New York Times report, the company expects capacity to exceed 3.5 gigawatts by the end of 2026, with plans to increase that figure to approximately 7 gigawatts in 2027. Such expansion highlights the substantial computing requirements associated with developing and operating increasingly sophisticated models. Meanwhile, Samsung Electronics reportedly plans to manufacture base dies for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips destined for Nvidia and AMD at its second foundry facility in Taylor, Texas. Construction is expected to begin this month, with mass production targeted for 2030. NVIDIA shares lost momentum early in September after failing to break decisively above the $236 resistance zone, with the rejection sending the stock back below $210 but we have seen a decent rebound recently. Shares have climbed above $233 today as investors responded positively to expanding infrastructure partnerships and CEO projections, but buyers are not able to sustain the rally above $243 and we saw dive to $200 again last week but we’re seeing some improvement today as NVDA finds support at the 50 weekly SMA. Competition is another concern for Nvidia. Google and Oracle recently announced plans to make Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) available through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure from 2027. This marks an important development because Google’s custom processors will become accessible through another major cloud platform, giving customers additional alternatives to Nvidia-powered systems. Nvidia maintains significant advantages through its established software ecosystem, performance and broad customer relationships. Nevertheless, Google’s expansion demonstrates that major technology companies are increasingly looking to reduce computing costs and dependence on external suppliers. If custom processors become more competitive, Nvidia could eventually face pressure on pricing and market share, even if overall computing demand continues growing. ASML reported record third-quarter sales of €11.7 billion but warned that planned semiconductor manufacturing capacity in 2027 and 2028 might not fully satisfy anticipated demand. The company forecast fourth-quarter revenue of €14.2 billion to €15.2 billion and narrowed its 2026 sales guidance to €44 billion–€45 billion. Manufacturing constraints could support semiconductor pricing, but they may also delay the equipment required to expand production. For Nvidia, these limitations could complicate supply arrangements and customers’ deployment schedules. Financing conditions are becoming increasingly important for the semiconductor industry. CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV) has experienced pressure after yields on its $1.25 billion bond issue due in 2032 reportedly reached 15% before closing near 14.5%. Such borrowing costs highlight the financial risks associated with building capital-intensive data centres. If financing becomes more expensive, operators could postpone projects or reduce expansion plans, eventually affecting Nvidia’s future orders. Electricity shortages present another obstacle. Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) reportedly has Nvidia-equipped server racks waiting in warehouses because some data centres lack sufficient electricity to operate them. Amazon’s Early Rack Receipt programme allows it to secure equipment before facilities are ready, but prolonged deployment delays could increase storage costs and postpone the generation of revenue from those investments. Nvidia continues to benefit from substantial demand for advanced processors, expanding infrastructure commitments and strategic relationships across the semiconductor industry. However, Google TPUs, financing pressures, manufacturing limitations and electricity shortages demonstrate that demand alone cannot guarantee continued growth. With NVDA recovering from approximately $200, investors will watch whether buyers can sustain momentum toward $220 and eventually challenge previous highs above $243. The larger trend remains sensitive to Big Tech spending decisions. If infrastructure costs continue increasing faster than the returns generated, customers could become more selective, creating additional pressure on Nvidia despite its leading position in the semiconductor market.

content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Shares of NVIDIA (NVDA) have lost 13.6% over the past month, while the S&P 500 lost 2.3%. Investors holding through the decline are likely betting that a wider market sell-off would pass quickly for NVIDIA, and that its unusually high profit margin will hold. So how deep have NVIDIA’s falls been when the whole market turned, and how long did they last? During a typical market shock, NVIDIA stock has fallen further than the S&P 500, and those declines have not always passed quickly. The company experienced its worst shock-driven drop since 2007 during the 2008-2009 financial crisis. NVIDIA lost 84% in that period, while the S&P 500 lost 53%. The stock also shed 63% in the 2022 inflation shock, against a 24% decline for the index. Across all the market shocks since 2007, the stock fell 28.1% on average, compared with 15.8% for the S&P 500. Measured from its lowest close, NVIDIA stock returned to its earlier high in a median of 1.6 months. Two recoveries took far longer. The stock needed 13.7 months to bounce back from the late-2018 growth scare, a period when it fell 56% against 19% for the S&P 500. It took 88 months, more than seven years, to recover from the 2008-2009 crisis. So far, NVIDIA’s margin is holding, and sales are growing alongside it. Revenue reached $303 billion over the four quarters to July 2026, up 83.4% from a year earlier. The company posted an operating margin of 65.2% over those twelve months, up from 58.1% a year before. No quarter end in the past ten years shows a higher operating margin. Debt has grown much faster than the business. Total debt for NVIDIA stood at $38.4 billion at the end of July 2026, up from $10.6 billion a year earlier. The company still covered that debt with its cash and short-term investments of $62.5 billion. Management’s own outlook, provided on the August 26, 2026 earnings call, already sets one market aside. That forecast includes no China data center compute revenue, given what management called ongoing geopolitical uncertainty. Shipments of Hopper 200 products to customers in China accounted for less than 1% of NVIDIA’s data center revenue in fiscal Q2 2027. NVIDIA is also putting its own balance sheet behind some customers. Management said the company has invested nearly $50 billion in frontier AI labs. The company expects demand from the labs it backs this way to make up roughly a quarter of its business in fiscal 2028, and management said it knows some will call this circular financing. Customers are also taking longer to pay. Management said NVIDIA’s days of sales outstanding, the time it takes to collect on a sale, rose to 60 days in fiscal Q2 2027, reflecting extended payment terms for large purchases. Margins at NVIDIA also face pressure from memory. Management said memory prices have risen more than it expected and are still heading higher. The company guided gross margin to 74%, plus or minus half a point, for fiscal Q3 2027, against 75% in fiscal Q2. Management expects margins to bottom at 71% to 72% in fiscal Q4, before settling at 72% to 73% in fiscal 2028 as its price increases take effect. Gross margin is the figure to watch when NVIDIA reports its fiscal Q3 2027 results in November 2026. The artificial intelligence (AI) trade has whipsawed this year, and so has its flagbearer Nvidia (NVDA). The chip-designing giant hit its record highs last month and has since lost 15% from those levels. As of last week's closing prices, the stock's year-to-date returns trail both the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index ($IUXX) and the diversified S&P 500 Index ($SPX). Nvidia's performance would seem at odds with its financial results, though. For instance, its revenues more than doubled in the most recent reported quarter, and its guidance for fiscal Q3 implies they will nearly double again. For the next fiscal year, Nvidia guided a 70% revenue growth, which is astonishing considering the high base. Moreover, at a time when companies are hard-pressed even to guide for the next quarter, Nvidia went out of its way to provide a forecast for the next fiscal year. Micron vs. SanDisk: China's DRAM Scare Hit Both Stocks, but 1 Is the Better Buy Ford and GM Are Taking Different Roads, but 1 Stock Races Ahead Nvidia Stock Looks Surprisingly Cheap. Why NVDA Could Rise 61%. Our exclusive Barchart Brief newsletter is your FREE midday guide to what's moving stocks, sectors, and investor sentiment - delivered right when you need the info most. Subscribe today! Following Nvidia's fiscal Q2 earnings release in August, I noted that despite the strong growth and reasonable valuations, Nvidia wasn't a "buy." With NVDA coming off those levels, let's explore the stock's outlook. The recent weakness in NVDA could be attributed to the weakness in the AI trade. Incidentally, all the Magnificent 7 names, which happen to be Nvidia's biggest customer set, plunged following their September quarter earnings, in part due to growing anxiety over their AI capex. Since much of this capex lands in Nvidia's coffers, the stock too fell alongside. To make things worse, Intel's (INTC) tepid Q4 guidance led to a sell-off in other chip stocks, which also put pressure on NVDA. On a broader level, there are concerns over the sustainability of Nvidia's growth since customers like Alphabet (GOOG) (GOOGL) and Amazon (AMZN) are working on their own chips. They are not only using them internally but also aggressively scouting third-party customers. Selling chips to third parties would help hyperscalers justify their burgeoning AI capex and offset some of their cash burn. Then there are fears over "circular financing" and off-balance-sheet financing. So, we have Nvidia investing in companies that buy its chips, while cloud companies like Amazon, Microsoft (MSFT), and Alphabet — the three biggest players in that order — are investing in AI startups that have developed into their biggest cloud customers, driving much of the incremental growth. While Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is dismissive of the very term circular financing and, during the Q2 call, said that he regrets not investing in these companies early, terming it an "once-in-a-generation opportunity," at least a section of the market is getting apprehensive over such transactions. Off-balance-sheet financing is another concern, and Nvidia has been providing credit guarantees for its customers' data centers. There are reports that Nvidia is in talks to provide credit guarantees to Nscale for a data center that Anthropic would use. Such deals add a layer of risk for Nvidia investors and would be catastrophic if AI actually turns out to be a bubble and goes bust. That, however, is not my base case assumption, and while there are visible signs of exuberance in AI, the technology holds a lot of promise. I believe the sell-off in NVDA stock has gone a bit too far and see the recent pullback as a buying opportunity, particularly as the company heads into its Q3 earnings call. While Nvidia's recent quarterly earnings have been followed by a decline in its stock price despite the company delivering a "beat and raise" quarter, the setup looks nice to me ahead of the Q3 report. At around the $200 price level, Nvidia is offering an attractive entry point with a price-to-earnings multiple of around 23x. While Nvidia has had a dismal run this year, I believe the stock should make up for it in the final two months of the year, and I see it ending the year higher than these levels. title: Nvidia Stock (NVDA) Falls 4.2% as Intel Outlook Hits Chips (Oct 30) - Gotrade
content: Gotrade News - In the latest Nvidia stock news, shares of Nvidia (NVDA) closed at $204.64 on Friday, October 30, 2026, down $9.02 or 4.22% in the US session. Financial media tied the Nvidia stock decline to a chip-wide selloff that followed Intel's weaker-than-expected guidance and renewed doubts about returns on AI spending. Regular-session close on Friday, October 30, 2026, 4:00 p.m. New York time. Stock prices: Yahoo Finance, cross-checked against the closing price on Nasdaq.com. Volume and 30-day average volume: Nasdaq.com. 52-week range: Yahoo Finance daily highs and lows since October 31, 2025. Indices and the 10-year Treasury yield: Yahoo Finance daily closes for the same date. Follow NVDA's latest price on our Nvidia (NVDA) stock price today page. Nvidia opened at $208.94, below the prior close, and slid as low as $200.92 before finishing $3.72 above that low. The day's high of $209.06 sat just above the open. Volume reached 168.4 million shares, 62.69% above the 103.5 million-share average. The decline was steeper than the broader market's. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.86% to 25,437.00, the S&P 500 lost 1.82% to 7,580.07 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 1.09% to 51,770.31, leaving Nvidia's move 1.36 percentage points worse than the Nasdaq's. The US 10-year Treasury yield fell 6.0 basis points to 4.93% in the same session. Within chips, Nvidia held up better than many peers. Intel (INTC) fell 28.58%, AMD dropped 10.88% and Marvell lost 10.05%, while Broadcom (AVGO), TSMC and Micron declined 5.48%, 5.95% and 5.30%. At the close, Nvidia stood 15.91% below its 52-week high and 24.58% above its 52-week low. None of the coverage reviewed for this article pointed to news from Nvidia itself; financial media tied the drop to a selloff across semiconductor stocks. According to CNBC, Intel shares had their worst day since the 1970s after the chipmaker guided to fourth-quarter adjusted earnings of 25 cents a share on revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, against analyst expectations of 43 cents and $17.1 billion. Intel cited a plant shutdown in Israel and softness in the PC market. As reported by Reuters, Intel's warning spread through the sector as investors weighed weakening PC demand, rising memory prices as suppliers shift production to AI chips, and AI infrastructure spending that is pushing tech giants toward borrowing. Matt Britzman, senior equity analyst at Hargreaves Lansdown, told Reuters investors were in a sell-first, ask-questions-later mood, and that Intel's warning gave them an easy reason to take profits across chip stocks. CNBC added that investors are questioning whether massive AI spending by tech giants will pay off, coming after Alphabet's worst day on record on Thursday. Nvidia's next earnings report is set for Tuesday, November 17, when the company will host a conference call at 2 p.m. PT on results for the third quarter of fiscal 2027, which ended October 25, 2026, according to Nvidia.
